archetype.name: Retooling Year (halfway back)
archetype.definition: After the 75-87 collapse of 2025, Baltimore rebuilt its run prevention and run differential to roughly league-average and finished honestly just under .500, but it never had the lineup depth to contend in a division where three teams won 87 or more.

report.headline: Halfway back from 2025: Alonso and a sound staff, too little lineup behind them

recap.finish: 79-82, fourth in the AL East, 19 games behind Tampa Bay; missed the postseason
recap.body:
This was a middle-of-the-league team, and its record matched its quality. Baltimore was outscored 739-718, a Run Diff / G of -0.13 that ranked 17th, and its W vs Run Diff of +0.6 says the 79 wins were about what it earned. In the league ranks it scored the 15th-most runs and allowed the 20th-fewest. That reads as mediocre, but it is a real step up from 2025, when a -0.69 differential was propped up by a +5.2 W vs Run Diff and the team ranked 25th on the site. This year it ranked 15th. The underlying team improved more than the four extra wins suggest.

The season was lost in May and June. After a .500 April, the staff gave up 156 runs in 29 May games, about 5.4 a night, and the club went 13-16. June was crueler in a different way: Baltimore scored and allowed exactly 122 runs and still went 11-16. By the end of June it sat at 39-48. July was the best stretch of the year, 15-8 while allowing just 94 runs. A 15-13 August pulled the club to 69-69. September (10-13, 3.9 runs scored per game) ended any push, including a home sweep by Milwaukee in which the Orioles scored one run across two of the three games.

The offense was Pete Alonso and a lot of roughly average at-bats. Alonso led the team with 5.0 WAR and a 148 wRC+, hit 43 homers with 113 RBI, and ranked first among first basemen on the site. Coby Mayo (112 wRC+, 24 HR) was the only other regular clearly above average. Gunnar Henderson played 158 games and was worth 3.6 WAR, though his bat was merely average at 101. Behind them, Leody Taveras (80 wRC+ in 482 PA), Jackson Holliday (81) and Jeremiah Jackson (67, with a .247 OBP) took a lot of plate appearances. The team OPS of .710 ranked 21st in a park that plays hitter-friendly (104), so the lineup was worse than its 15th-ranked run total looks. Hence the C grade.

Run prevention carried the improvement. Team ERA dropped from 4.60 to 4.07, 12th in the league, and Fielding Runs climbed from -26.7 to -3.7. Trevor Rogers (4.0 WAR, 3.45 FIP, 5.6% walk rate) and Shane Baz (3.4 WAR, 3.62 FIP) gave the rotation a legitimate front two. The rest was thinner: Kyle Bradish walked 10.5% and ended on the 60-day injured list, and Chris Bassitt posted a 1.55 WHIP, so the group graded C. The bullpen earned a B. Yennier Cano (2.90 ERA, 2.78 FIP) and Rico Garcia (10 saves, 19 holds) handled the late innings, and Grant Wolfram's 2.66 FIP says his 4.30 ERA undersold him.

The ending was a fair verdict. A team that is outscored by 21 runs over a season doesn't belong in October, and this one didn't fall short because of bad luck. It finished eight games behind third-place Boston and well clear of nothing but Toronto.

highlights.title: Alonso carried the lineup
highlights.body: Alonso was the best first baseman on the site: 43 homers, a 148 wRC+ and 5.0 WAR over 161 games. He was the only hitter who reliably drove the offense. Mayo's 112 wRC+ was the next-best mark among regulars. The production is real, but a lineup that depends this heavily on one bat has no margin when he slumps.

highlights.title: A real front two and a solid bullpen
highlights.body: Rogers and Baz combined for 7.4 WAR over about 349 innings. Both had FIPs well under their ERAs, which suggests their run prevention can hold or improve. The bullpen graded B behind Cano and Garcia, and Wolfram's peripherals point to better results ahead. Together they pulled team ERA into the top half of the league.

highlights.title: The defense stopped bleeding runs
highlights.body: Fielding Runs went from -26.7 in 2025 to -3.7. That is a gain of roughly 23 runs, which by itself accounts for much of the improvement in run differential. Cowser (+6.8 Def Runs) and Basallo (+2.6) helped. Beavers at -7.2 shows there is still a soft spot in the outfield.

lowlights.title: Too many weak bats in the lineup
lowlights.body: Three regulars with 290 or more PA posted a wRC+ of 81 or below, and Jackson's .247 OBP was a hole at the bottom of the order. In a park that favors hitters, a .710 team OPS ranked 21st. Unless that depth improves, the offense stays one-dimensional.

lowlights.title: May and June sank the season
lowlights.body: The staff allowed 156 runs in May. June then produced an 11-16 record despite a dead-even run total, which cost a couple of games to sequencing. The 39-48 hole at the end of June was too deep for the 30-21 July-August run to climb out of.

lowlights.title: The back of the rotation is fragile
lowlights.body: Brandon Young's 3.56 ERA sits against a 4.47 FIP, so some regression is likely. Bradish walked 10.5% and finished on the 60-day injured list. Bassitt's 1.55 WHIP made him hittable. Beyond Rogers and Baz, the rotation is less sturdy than its ERA looks.

arc.note: After a .500 April, Baltimore slid to 39-48 through May and June. It surged to 69-69 on a 15-8 July and a winning August, then faded with a 10-13 September.

recap.nextYear: There is little luck to unwind in this record: a +0.6 W vs Run Diff means 79-82 is who this team was. The foundation is Alonso's bat, Rogers and Baz at the top of the rotation, and a B bullpen whose peripherals (Wolfram, Cano) look sustainable. The concerns are Young's ERA running well ahead of his FIP, Bradish ending on the injured list, and a lineup where Henderson, Basallo, Holliday and the outfield corners all hovered at or below average. The run prevention gains, especially the roughly 23-run swing in fielding, look real. But with Tampa Bay, New York and Boston all at 87 wins or more, closing a 21-run deficit requires at least two more above-average bats, not just repeating this year.
